newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK annual RPI seen easing in August.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK annual RPI seen easing in August.

text.p: UK retail price inflation is forecast to ease fractionally in August, with the yearly headline and underlying rates both shedding about 0.1 percentage points. August data are due on Thursday.
A Reuter poll of economists produced a consensus forecast for headline August inflation of 2.1 percent year-on-year, down from 2.2 in July. That equates to a 0.4 percent monthly rise.
The core rate, excluding mortgage payments (RPIX), is expected to slip to 2.7 percent year-on-year from 2.8 in July.
"We expect no change in inflation in August," analysts at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.

"Although we stick with our view that retail inflation will fall to below 2.5 percent in coming months, aided by lower upstream pressures, there are offsetting forces this month," they said in a client note.
Details of the figures are likely to show conflicting forces at work.
David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, said a rebound in seasonal food prices month-on-month was likely in August following a sharp 9.1 percent drop in July.
However, lower mortgage rates, following the official interest rate cut in June, will cut the headline inflation rate, although not the core one.
A large rise in seasonal food prices in August 1995 will drop out of the year-on-year figures, according to Philip Uglow, economist at Union Plc.
In contrast, an unwinding of summer sales discounts and rising petrol prices will put upward pressure on prices, he said.

Following another benign producer price report on Monday, year-on-year output price inflation is now at its lowest level since July 1994, while year-on-year core output prices are at nearly 30-year lows.

"July's data revealed some worrying signs that service sector inflation was picking up, but this should be more than offset in the short-term...by the recent collapse in factory gate inflation," Philpotts said.

While a subdued retail price report should come as no surprise, this does not necessarily mean it will help Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, should he wish to squeeze in one last interest rate cut.
"If there is to be another rate cut we would need unequivocally weak data or a tight budget, and Clarke is bound to want to cut taxes in pre-election mode," said Uglow.
Clarke will present his budget on November 26 in the run-up to elections that must be held by May 1997.
